title: L'Hopital's Rule and When It Is Legal
quickIdea: L'Hopital replaces f/g by f'/g' - but only for 0/0 or infinity/infinity, only near the point, and only when the new limit exists.
remember: The rule applies to lim f(x)/g(x) only when the form is 0/0 or infinity/infinity at the point.
Differentiate the numerator and the denominator separately. Never apply the quotient rule to the whole fraction.
The rule may be repeated while each new ratio is still 0/0 or infinity/infinity.
The rule is valid only if lim f'/g' exists (as a finite number or as +-infinity). If f'/g' oscillates, the rule tells you nothing about the original limit.
Check by substitution first. If substitution gives a number, that number is the limit and L'Hopital must not be used.
One application is often cheaper than two: simplify between applications rather than differentiating twice.

example.work: At x = 1: numerator 1 - 2 + 1 = 0 and denominator 1 - 3 + 2 = 0, so the form is 0/0. Differentiate separately: numerator 7x^6 - 10x^4, denominator 3x^2 - 6x. At x = 1 these are 7 - 10 = -3 and 3 - 6 = -3. The ratio is (-3)/(-3) = 1.
example.answer: The limit is 1. Both one-sided limits give the same value, so the two-sided limit exists.

gateAngle: This is the single most used technique in the topic: 2019 Q.13, 2017 Set 1 Q.28, 2021 Set 1 Q.20, 2022 Q.24 and 2016 Set 1 Q.3 all yield to it in one or two applications. 2021 Set 1 Q.20 is also the reminder that rationalising the numerator gives the same answer - the papers accept whichever is faster.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: Evaluate lim(x->1) (x^3 - 1)/(x^2 - 1).
variations.answer: 3/2. Both parts vanish at 1, so differentiate: 3x^2/(2x) at x = 1 gives 3/2. Factoring gives the same: (x^2 + x + 1)/(x + 1) at 1 is 3/2.
variations.why: Two routes to one number is the check GATE rewards: factor when the degree is small, differentiate when it is not.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: Why is L'Hopital's rule invalid on lim(x->1) (x^2 + 1)/(x + 1)?
variations.answer: Because the form is not indeterminate: at x = 1 the ratio is 2/2 = 1. Differentiating would give 2x/1 = 2 at x = 1, which is simply a different quantity.
variations.why: The rule is a theorem about 0/0 and infinity/infinity only. Applying it elsewhere produces a number that looks plausible and is wrong.

variations.label: PREDICTED VARIATION
variations.question: Evaluate lim(x->0+) sqrt(x)/(1 - e^(2 sqrt(x))).
variations.answer: -1/2. This is GATE CSE 2022 Q.24; substitute u = 2 sqrt(x) to get -1/2 * u/(e^u - 1), whose second factor tends to 1.
variations.why: The 2022 question looks like a one-sided L'Hopital problem but is faster as a substitution into the standard limit (e^u - 1)/u -> 1. Recognising which of the two tools is cheaper is the revision point.

trap.what: Applying L'Hopital when the form is not indeterminate, or trusting it when the ratio of derivatives has no limit.
trap.why: The rule is an implication, not an equivalence: if the derivative ratio has a limit then it equals the original limit, and nothing is claimed otherwise. Non-indeterminate forms are outside the theorem entirely.
trap.counterexample: lim(x->inf) (x + sin x)/x equals 1, but the derivative ratio is (1 + cos x)/1, which oscillates and has no limit. The rule fails; dividing numerator and denominator by x succeeds. Separately, lim(x->1) (x^2 + 1)/(x + 1) = 1 while the derivative ratio at 1 is 2.

check.question: Use L'Hopital's rule to evaluate lim(x->0) (1 - cos x)/x^2.
check.explanation: The form is 0/0. One application gives sin x/(2x), still 0/0. A second gives cos x/2, which at 0 is 1/2. Both applications were legal because each intermediate ratio was indeterminate.
